chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter XIX
paragraphs: On the twenty-fourth of August the battle of the Shevardino Redoubt was fought; on the twenty-fifth not a shot was fired by either side; and on the twenty-sixth the battle of Borodino itself took place.

Why and how were the battles of Shevardino and Borodino fought and accepted? Why was the battle of Borodino fought? There was not the slightest sense in it for either the French or the Russians. Its immediate result for the Russians was, and was bound to be, that we were brought closer to the destruction of Moscow—which we feared more than anything in the world; and for the French, its immediate result was that they were brought closer to the destruction of their whole army—which they feared more than anything in the world. The outcome was completely obvious, and yet Napoleon offered and Kutuzov accepted the battle.

If the commanders had been guided by reason, it would seem obvious to Napoleon that by advancing thirteen hundred miles and fighting with a probability of losing a quarter of his army, he was marching toward certain destruction; and it would have been equally clear to Kutuzov that by accepting battle and risking the loss of a quarter of his army, he would certainly lose Moscow. For Kutuzov this was mathematically clear, just as it is clear in checkers that if I have one piece less and keep trading, I will certainly lose—and therefore should not trade. When my opponent has sixteen pieces and I have fourteen, I am only one-eighth weaker; but when I have traded away thirteen more, he will be three times as strong as I am.

Before the battle of Borodino our strength relative to the French was about five to six, but after the battle it was little more than one to two: before the battle we had a hundred thousand against a hundred and twenty thousand; afterward, barely fifty thousand against a hundred thousand. Yet the shrewd and experienced Kutuzov accepted the battle, while Napoleon, supposedly a commander of genius, offered it—losing a quarter of his army and stretching his supply lines even further. If we are told he expected to end the campaign by capturing Moscow, as he had ended a previous campaign by capturing Vienna, there is much evidence to the contrary. Napoleon's own historians tell us that from Smolensk onward he wanted to stop, that he knew the danger of his extended position, and that he knew the occupation of Moscow would not end the campaign, for he had seen at Smolensk the state in which Russian towns were being left to him, and had received not a single reply to his repeated proposals to negotiate.

In giving and accepting battle at Borodino, Kutuzov acted involuntarily and irrationally. But later, to fit what had occurred, historians provided cleverly crafted evidence of the foresight and genius of the generals who, of all the blind tools of history, were the most enslaved and involuntary.

The ancients left us model heroic poems in which the heroes supply the entire interest of the story, and we are still unable to accustom ourselves to the fact that for our era, such histories are meaningless.

On the other question—how the battles of Borodino and Shevardino were actually fought—there also exists a definite, well-known, but quite false account. All the historians describe the affair as follows:
The Russian army, they say, in its retreat from Smolensk, sought the best position for a general battle and found it at Borodino.

The Russians, they say, fortified this position in advance on the left of the highway (from Moscow to Smolensk) and almost at right angles to it, from Borodino to Utitsa, at the very place where the battle was fought.

In front of this position, they say, a fortified outpost was established on the Shevardino mound to observe the enemy. On the twenty-fourth, we are told, Napoleon attacked this advanced post and took it, and on the twenty-sixth attacked the whole Russian army, which was in position on the field of Borodino.
So the histories say, and it is all quite wrong, as anyone who cares to examine the matter can easily see.

The Russians did not seek the best position; on the contrary, during the retreat they passed many positions better than Borodino. They did not stop at any of them because Kutuzov did not wish to occupy a position he had not chosen himself, because the popular demand for battle had not yet been expressed strongly enough, because Miloradovich had not yet arrived with the militia, and for many other reasons. The fact is that other positions they had passed were stronger, and the position at Borodino (where the battle was fought), far from being strong, was no more of a position than any other random spot in the Russian Empire.

Not only did the Russians not fortify the position on the field of Borodino to the left of and at right angles to the highway (the position where the battle took place), but never until the twenty-fifth of August, 1812, did they even consider that a battle might be fought there. This is shown, first, by the fact that there were no entrenchments there by the twenty-fifth, and those begun on the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth were never completed; and second, by the position of the Shevardino Redoubt. That redoubt was quite senseless as an outpost of the position where the battle was actually accepted. Why was it more heavily fortified than any other point? And why were all efforts exhausted and six thousand men sacrificed defending it until late at night on the twenty-fourth? A Cossack patrol would have sufficed to observe the enemy. Third, as proof that the position where the battle was fought had not been planned, and that the Shevardino Redoubt was not an advanced post of that position, we have the fact that until the twenty-fifth, both Barclay de Tolly and Bagration believed the Shevardino Redoubt was the left flank of the position, and that Kutuzov himself, in his report written hastily after the battle, calls the Shevardino Redoubt the left flank of the position. It was only much later, when reports on the battle of Borodino were written at leisure, that the incorrect and extraordinary claim was invented (probably to justify the mistakes of a commander in chief who had to be portrayed as infallible) that the Shevardino Redoubt was an advanced post—whereas in reality it was simply a fortified point on the left flank—and that the battle of Borodino was fought on a pre-selected, entrenched position, whereas it was actually fought on a nearly unexpected and almost unfortified spot.

The situation was clearly this: a position was selected along the river Kolocha—which crosses the highway not at a right angle but at an acute angle—so that the left flank was at Shevardino, the right flank near the village of Novoe, and the center at Borodino at the confluence of the Kolocha and Voyna rivers.

To anyone looking at the field of Borodino without considering how the battle was actually fought, this position, protected by the river Kolocha, seems the obvious one for an army trying to prevent an enemy from advancing along the Smolensk road to Moscow.

Napoleon, riding to Valuevo on the twenty-fourth, did not see (as the history books claim) the Russian position from Utitsa to Borodino (he could not have seen that position because it did not exist), nor did he see an advanced post of the Russian army. Instead, while pursuing the Russian rearguard, he came upon the left flank of the Russian position—at the Shevardino Redoubt—and unexpectedly moved his army across the Kolocha. The Russians, not having time to begin a general battle, pulled back their left wing from the position they had intended to hold and took up a new position that had not been planned and was not fortified. By crossing the Kolocha to the left of the highway, Napoleon shifted the entire coming battle from right to left (from the Russian perspective) and transferred it to the plain between Utitsa, Semenovsk, and Borodino—a plain no more advantageous than any other in Russia—and there the entire battle of the twenty-sixth of August took place.

Had Napoleon not ridden out on the evening of the twenty-fourth to the Kolocha, and had he not then ordered an immediate attack on the redoubt but instead begun the attack the next morning, no one would have doubted that the Shevardino Redoubt was the left flank of our position, and the battle would have taken place where we expected. In that case, we would probably have defended the Shevardino Redoubt—our left flank—even more stubbornly. We would have attacked Napoleon in the center or on the right, and the battle would have been fought on the twenty-fifth in the position we had intended and fortified. But since the attack on our left flank came in the evening after the retreat of our rearguard (that is, immediately after the fight at Gridneva), and since the Russian commanders could not or would not begin a general engagement on the evening of the twenty-fourth, the first and decisive action of the battle of Borodino was already lost on the twenty-fourth, and this obviously led to the loss of the one fought on the twenty-sixth.

After the loss of the Shevardino Redoubt, we found ourselves on the morning of the twenty-fifth without a position for our left flank, and were forced to bend it back and hastily entrench it wherever it happened to be.

Not only was the Russian army on the twenty-sixth defended by weak, unfinished entrenchments, but the disadvantage of that position was increased by the fact that the Russian commanders—not having fully grasped what had happened, namely the loss of our position on the left flank and the shifting of the entire battlefield from right to left—maintained their extended position from the village of Novoe to Utitsa, and consequently had to shift their forces from right to left during the battle. So throughout the entire battle, the Russians opposed the entire French army launched against our left flank with only half as many men. (Poniatowski's action against Utitsa and Uvarov's on the right flank against the French were separate actions from the main battle.) So the battle of Borodino was not fought at all as it has been described (in an effort to conceal the commanders' mistakes, even at the cost of diminishing the glory due to the Russian army and people). The battle of Borodino was not fought on a pre-chosen, entrenched position with forces only slightly weaker than the enemy's. Rather, as a result of the loss of the Shevardino Redoubt, the Russians fought the battle of Borodino on an open and almost unfortified position, with forces only half as numerous as the French—that is, under conditions in which it was not merely unthinkable to fight for ten hours and achieve an indecisive result, but unthinkable to keep an army from complete collapse and rout.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter XX
paragraphs: On the morning of the twenty-fifth, Pierre was leaving Mozhaysk. At the descent of the high, steep hill where a winding road led out of town past the cathedral on the right—where a service was being held and the bells were ringing—Pierre got out of his carriage and continued on foot. Behind him a cavalry regiment was coming down the hill, preceded by its singers. Coming up toward him was a train of carts carrying men wounded in the previous day's engagement. The peasant drivers, shouting and lashing their horses, kept crossing from side to side. The carts, each holding three or four wounded soldiers lying or sitting, jolted over the stones thrown on the steep slope to form something like a road. The wounded, bandaged with rags, with pale cheeks, compressed lips, and knitted brows, gripped the sides of the carts as they jolted against one another. Almost all of them stared with naive, childlike curiosity at Pierre's white hat and green tailcoat.

Pierre's coachman shouted angrily at the convoy of wounded to keep to one side of the road. The cavalry regiment, descending the hill with its singers, surrounded Pierre's carriage and blocked the road. Pierre stopped, pressed against the side of the road cut into the hillside. The sunshine from behind the hill didn't reach into the cut, and there it was cold and damp, but above Pierre's head was the bright August sun and the bells rang merrily. One of the carts of wounded stopped by the roadside close to Pierre. The driver in his bast shoes ran panting up to it, placed a stone under one of the rear wheels, and began adjusting the harness on his small horse.
One of the wounded, an old soldier with a bandaged arm who was walking alongside the cart, caught hold of it with his good hand and turned to look at Pierre.
"I say, countryman! Will they set us down here or take us on to Moscow?" he asked.

Pierre was so deep in thought that he didn't hear the question. He was looking now at the cavalry regiment that had met the convoy of wounded, now at the cart beside him, in which two wounded men were sitting and one was lying. One of those sitting up had probably been hit in the cheek. His whole head was wrapped in bandages and one cheek was swollen to the size of a baby's head. His nose and mouth were twisted to one side. This soldier was looking at the cathedral and crossing himself. Another, a young recruit as pale as if there were no blood in his thin face, looked at Pierre kindly with a fixed smile. The third lay face down so that his face was hidden. The cavalry singers were passing close by:
Ah lost, quite lost... is my head so keen, Living in a foreign land...
they sang their soldiers' marching song.

As if in response to them, but with a different kind of merriment, the metallic sound of the bells rang out high above, and the hot rays of the sun bathed the top of the opposite slope with yet another sort of joy. But below the slope, by the cart with the wounded and the panting little horse where Pierre stood, it was damp, somber, and sad.
The soldier with the swollen cheek looked angrily at the cavalry singers.
"Oh, the show-offs!" he muttered reproachfully.

"It's not just the soldiers—I've seen peasants today too... The peasants—even they have to go," said the soldier behind the cart, addressing Pierre with a sad smile. "No distinctions nowadays... They want the whole nation to attack them—in a word, it's Moscow! They want to make an end of it."
Despite the vagueness of the soldier's words, Pierre understood what he meant and nodded in agreement.
The road cleared again; Pierre descended the hill and drove on.

He kept looking to either side of the road for familiar faces but saw only the unfamiliar faces of soldiers from various branches of the service, all of whom stared with astonishment at his white hat and green tailcoat.

Having gone nearly three miles, he at last met an acquaintance and eagerly called out to him. This was one of the senior army doctors. He was driving toward Pierre in a covered gig, sitting beside a young surgeon, and on recognizing Pierre told the Cossack in the driver's seat to stop.
"Count! Your excellency, what brings you here?" asked the doctor.
"Well, you know, I wanted to see..."
"Yes, yes, there will be something to see..."
Pierre got out and talked to the doctor, explaining his intention of being present at the battle.
The doctor advised him to apply directly to Kutuzov.

"Why should you be God knows where, out of sight, during the battle?" he said, exchanging glances with his young companion. "In any case, his Serene Highness knows you and will receive you graciously. That's what you must do."
The doctor seemed tired and in a hurry.
"You think so?... I also wanted to ask—where exactly is our position?" said Pierre.
"The position?" the doctor repeated. "Well, that's not my area. Drive past Tatarinova; there's a lot of digging going on there. Go up the hill and you'll see."
"You can see from there?... If you would..."
But the doctor interrupted him and moved toward his gig.

"I'd go with you, but honestly I'm up to here"—he pointed to his throat. "I'm racing to the corps commander. How do things stand?... You know, Count, there'll be a battle tomorrow. Out of a hundred thousand, we must expect at least twenty thousand wounded, and we haven't enough stretchers, beds, medics, or doctors for six thousand. We have ten thousand carts, but we need other things too—we'll just have to manage."

The strange thought that of the thousands of men—young and old—who had stared with cheerful surprise at his hat (perhaps the very men he had noticed), twenty thousand were doomed to wounds and death, struck Pierre forcefully.

"They may die tomorrow; why are they thinking about anything but death?" And by some hidden chain of thought, the descent of the Mozhaysk hill, the carts with the wounded, the ringing bells, the slanting rays of the sun, and the cavalrymen's songs vividly recurred to him.

"The cavalry ride to battle and meet the wounded and don't give a moment's thought to what awaits them, but ride past winking at the wounded. Yet from among these men, twenty thousand are doomed to die—and they wonder at my hat! Strange!" thought Pierre, continuing toward Tatarinova.

In front of a landowner's house to the left of the road stood carriages, wagons, and crowds of orderlies and sentries. The commander in chief was staying there, but when Pierre arrived he was not in, and hardly any of the staff were present—they had gone to the church service. Pierre drove on toward Gorki.

When he had climbed the hill and reached the little village street, he saw for the first time peasant militiamen in their white shirts and with crosses on their caps, who, talking and laughing loudly, lively and sweating, were at work on a huge knoll overgrown with grass to the right of the road.
Some of them were digging, others wheeling barrowloads of earth along planks, while others stood around doing nothing.

Two officers stood on the knoll directing the men. Seeing these peasants, who were clearly still amused by the novelty of their position as soldiers, Pierre once again thought of the wounded at Mozhaysk and understood what the soldier had meant when he said: "They want the whole nation to attack them." The sight of these bearded peasants working on the battlefield, with their clumsy boots, sweating necks, and shirts open from the left to the middle, exposing their sunburned collarbones, impressed Pierre more powerfully with the solemnity and importance of the moment than anything he had yet seen or heard.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter XXI
paragraphs: Pierre got out of his carriage and, passing the toiling militiamen, climbed the knoll from which, according to the doctor, the battlefield could be seen.
It was about eleven o'clock. The sun was somewhat to the left and behind him, and brightly illuminated the enormous panorama that rose like an amphitheater before him in the clear, thin air.

From the upper left, cutting through that amphitheater, wound the Smolensk highway, passing through a village with a white church about five hundred paces ahead of the knoll and below it. This was Borodino. Below the village the road crossed the river by a bridge and, winding down and up, rose higher and higher to the village of Valuevo, visible about four miles away, where Napoleon was then stationed. Beyond Valuevo the road vanished into a yellowing forest on the horizon. Far in the distance in that birch and fir forest to the right of the road, the cross and belfry of the Kolocha Monastery gleamed in the sun. Scattered over the whole blue expanse, to right and left of the forest and the road, smoking campfires could be seen and indistinct masses of troops—ours and the enemy's. The ground to the right—along the course of the Kolocha and Moskva rivers—was broken and hilly. Between the hollows, the villages of Bezubova and Zakharino were visible in the distance. On the left the ground was more level; there were grain fields, and the smoking ruins of Semenovsk, which had been burned, could be seen.

Everything Pierre saw was so indistinct that neither the left nor the right side of the field matched what he had expected. Nowhere could he see the battlefield he had imagined—only fields, meadows, troops, woods, campfire smoke, villages, hills, and streams; and try as he might, he could make out no military "position" in this place teeming with life, nor could he even tell our troops from the enemy's.
"I need to ask someone who knows," he thought, and approached an officer who was looking with curiosity at his huge, unmilitary figure.
"May I ask," said Pierre, "what village that is ahead?"
"Burdino, isn't it?" said the officer, turning to his companion.
"Borodino," the other corrected him.
The officer, clearly glad of a chance to talk, moved up to Pierre.
"Are those our men there?" Pierre asked.
"Yes, and farther on are the French," said the officer. "There they are, there... you can see them."
"Where? Where?" asked Pierre.
"You can see them with the naked eye... Look, there!"
The officer pointed toward the smoke visible to the left beyond the river, and the same stern and serious expression Pierre had noticed on many faces that day came over his own.
"Ah, those are the French! And over there?" Pierre pointed to a knoll on the left, near which some troops were visible.
"Those are ours."
"And there?" Pierre pointed to another knoll in the distance with a big tree on it, near a village in a hollow where campfires were smoking and something dark could be seen.
"That's his again," said the officer. (It was the Shevardino Redoubt.) "It was ours yesterday, but now it's his."
"Then where's our position?"

"Our position?" replied the officer with a satisfied smile. "I can tell you quite clearly, because I built nearly all our fortifications. There, you see? There's our center, at Borodino, right there," and he pointed to the village with the white church ahead. "That's where you cross the Kolocha. You see down there where the rows of hay are in the hollow? That's the bridge. That's our center. Our right flank is over there"—he pointed sharply to the right, far away in the broken ground—"that's where the Moskva River is, and we've built three very strong redoubts there. The left flank..." Here the officer paused. "Well, you see, that's harder to explain... Yesterday our left flank was there at Shevardino, you see, where the oak is, but now we've pulled our left wing back—now it's over there, do you see that village and the smoke? That's Semenovsk, yes, there," he pointed to Raevsky's knoll. "But the battle probably won't be there. His having moved his troops there is just a feint; he'll probably swing around to the right of the Moskva. But wherever it may be, many a man won't be here tomorrow!" he added.
An elderly sergeant who had come up while the officer was speaking had waited silently for him to finish, but at this point, evidently not liking the officer's remark, interrupted him.
"Gabions need to be sent for," he said sternly.
The officer looked embarrassed, as though he understood one might think about how many men would be missing tomorrow but shouldn't say it aloud.
"Well, send third company again," the officer said quickly.
"And you—are you one of the doctors?"
"No, I've come on my own," answered Pierre, and he went back down the hill, passing the militiamen.
"Oh, those damned fellows!" muttered the officer, following him and holding his nose as he ran past the working men.
"There they are... bringing her, coming... There they are... They'll be here in a minute..." voices were suddenly heard, and officers, soldiers, and militiamen began running forward along the road.
A church procession was coming up the hill from Borodino. First along the dusty road came infantry in ranks, bareheaded and with arms reversed. From behind them came the sound of church singing.
Soldiers and militiamen ran bareheaded past Pierre toward the procession.
"They're bringing her—our Protectress!... The Iberian Mother of God!" someone cried.
"The Smolensk Mother of God," another corrected him.

The militiamen—both those who had been in the village and those who had been working on the battery—threw down their shovels and ran to meet the church procession. Following the battalion that marched along the dusty road came priests in their vestments—one little old man in a hood with attendants and singers. Behind them, soldiers and officers carried a large, dark-faced icon in an embossed metal cover. This was the icon that had been brought from Smolensk and had since accompanied the army. Behind, before, and on both sides, crowds of militiamen with bared heads walked, ran, and bowed to the ground.

At the top of the hill they stopped with the icon; the men who had been holding it up by the linen bands were relieved by others, the chanters relit their censers, and the service began. The hot rays of the sun beat straight down, and a fresh soft wind played with the hair of the bared heads and with the ribbons decorating the icon. The singing didn't sound loud under the open sky. An immense crowd of bareheaded officers, soldiers, and militiamen surrounded the icon. Behind the priest and chanter stood the dignitaries in a reserved spot. A bald general with a Saint George's Cross on his neck stood just behind the priest, and without crossing himself (he was evidently a German) patiently waited for the service to end, which he considered it necessary to attend, probably to arouse the Russian people's patriotism. Another general stood in a martial pose, crossing himself with a quick motion of his hand before his chest while looking about him. Standing among the crowd of peasants, Pierre recognized several acquaintances among these notables but didn't look at them—his whole attention was absorbed by the serious expression on the faces of the soldiers and militiamen, who were all gazing intently at the icon. As soon as the tired chanters, who were singing the service for the twentieth time that day, began lazily and mechanically to sing, "Save from calamity Your servants, O Mother of God," and the priest and deacon chimed in, "For to You under God we all flee as to an unbreakable wall and protection," there again kindled in all those faces the same expression of awareness of the solemnity of the approaching moment that Pierre had seen at the foot of the hill at Mozhaysk and fleetingly on the many faces he had met that morning; and heads bowed more often, hair was tossed back, and sighs and the sound of men crossing themselves were heard.
The crowd around the icon suddenly parted and pressed against Pierre. Someone—a very important person, judging by the haste with which way was made—was approaching the icon.
It was Kutuzov, who had been riding around the position and on his way back to Tatarinova had stopped where the service was being held. Pierre recognized him at once by his distinctive figure.

With a long overcoat on his extremely stout, round-shouldered body, with his uncovered white head and puffy face showing the white ball of the eye he had lost, Kutuzov walked with a plunging, swaying gait into the crowd and stopped behind the priest. He crossed himself with a practiced movement, reached down and touched the ground with his hand, and bowed his white head with a deep sigh. Behind Kutuzov was Bennigsen and the suite. Despite the commander in chief's presence, which attracted the attention of all the senior officers, the militiamen and soldiers continued their prayers without looking at him.

When the service was over, Kutuzov stepped up to the icon, sank heavily to his knees, bowed to the ground, and for a long time tried in vain to rise but could not because of his weakness and weight. His white head twitched with the effort. At last he rose, kissed the icon as a child does with naively pouting lips, and again bowed until he touched the ground with his hand. The other generals followed his example, then the officers, and after them, with excited faces, pressing on one another, crowding, panting, and pushing, came the soldiers and militiamen.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter XXII
paragraphs: Staggering amid the crush, Pierre looked around.
"Count Peter Kirilych! How did you get here?" said a voice.

Pierre looked round. Boris Drubetskoy, brushing his knees with his hand (he had probably dirtied them kneeling before the icon), came up to him smiling. Boris was elegantly dressed with a slightly military flair appropriate to a campaign. He wore a long coat and, like Kutuzov, had a whip slung across his shoulder.

Meanwhile Kutuzov had reached the village and seated himself in the shade of the nearest house, on a bench that one Cossack had run to fetch and another had hastily covered with a rug. An immense and brilliant suite surrounded him.
The icon was carried farther, accompanied by the crowd. Pierre stopped some thirty paces from Kutuzov, talking to Boris.
He explained his wish to be present at the battle and see the position.

"This is what you must do," said Boris. "I'll show you around the camp. You'll see everything best from where Count Bennigsen will be. I'm in attendance on him, you know; I'll mention it to him. But if you want to ride around the position, come with us. We're just going to the left flank. Then when we get back, please spend the night with me and we'll arrange a game of cards. Of course you know Dmitri Sergeevich? Those are his quarters," and he pointed to the third house in the village of Gorki.
"But I'd like to see the right flank. They say it's very strong," said Pierre. "I'd like to start from the Moskva River and ride around the whole position."
"Well, you can do that later, but the main thing is the left flank."
"Yes, yes. But where is Prince Bolkonsky's regiment? Can you show me?"
"Prince Andrew's? We'll pass it, and I'll take you to him."
"What about the left flank?" asked Pierre.

"To tell you the truth, between us, God only knows what shape our left flank is in," said Boris confidentially, lowering his voice. "It's not at all what Count Bennigsen intended. He meant to fortify that knoll quite differently, but..." Boris shrugged. "His Serene Highness wouldn't have it, or someone talked him out of it. You see..." But Boris didn't finish, because at that moment Kaisarov, Kutuzov's adjutant, came up to Pierre. "Ah, Kaisarov!" said Boris, addressing him with an easy smile. "I was just trying to explain our position to the count. It's amazing how his Serene Highness foresaw the French intentions!"
"You mean the left flank?" asked Kaisarov.
"Yes, exactly; the left flank is now extremely strong."

Though Kutuzov had dismissed all unnecessary people from the staff, Boris had managed to stay on at headquarters after the changes. He had attached himself to Count Bennigsen, who, like everyone Boris had ever attended, considered young Prince Drubetskoy an invaluable man.

In the higher command there were two sharply defined parties: Kutuzov's and Bennigsen's. Boris belonged to the latter, and while showing servile respect to Kutuzov, he skillfully created the impression that the old man wasn't up to much and that Bennigsen was running everything. Now the decisive moment of battle had come, when Kutuzov would either be discredited and power would pass to Bennigsen, or even if Kutuzov won, it would be felt that everything was Bennigsen's doing. In either case, many great rewards would be given for the next day's action, and new men would come to the fore. So Boris was full of nervous energy all day.

After Kaisarov, other people Pierre knew came up to him, and he hadn't time to answer all the questions about Moscow showered on him or to listen to everything they told him. All faces expressed excitement and apprehension, but it seemed to Pierre that the excitement in some of these faces was mainly about questions of personal advancement; his own mind, however, was occupied by the different expression he saw on other faces—an expression that spoke not of personal matters but of the universal questions of life and death. Kutuzov noticed Pierre's figure and the group gathered around him.
"Call him to me," said Kutuzov.
An aide told Pierre of his Serene Highness's wish, and Pierre went toward Kutuzov's bench. But a militiaman got there before him. It was Dolokhov.
"How did that fellow get here?" asked Pierre.

"He's a creature that worms his way in everywhere!" was the answer. "He was demoted, you know. Now he wants to claw his way back. He's been proposing some scheme or other and has crawled into the enemy's picket line at night... He's a brave fellow, though."
Pierre took off his hat and bowed respectfully to Kutuzov.
"I concluded that if I reported to your Serene Highness, you might send me away or say that you already knew what I was reporting, but then I wouldn't lose anything..." Dolokhov was saying.
"Yes, yes."
"But if I were right, I'd be rendering a service to my Fatherland, for which I'm ready to die."
"Yes, yes."
"And should your Serene Highness need a man who won't spare his skin, please think of me... Perhaps I may prove useful to your Serene Highness."
"Yes... yes..." Kutuzov repeated, his laughing eye narrowing more and more as he looked at Pierre.

Just then Boris, with his courtier's skill, stepped up to Pierre near Kutuzov and in the most natural manner, without raising his voice, said to Pierre as though continuing an interrupted conversation:
"The militia have put on clean white shirts to be ready to die. What heroism, Count!"
Boris clearly said this to Pierre intending to be overheard by his Serene Highness. He knew Kutuzov's attention would be caught by those words, and it was.
"What are you saying about the militia?" he asked Boris.
"Preparing for tomorrow, your Serene Highness—for death—they've put on clean shirts."
"Ah... a wonderful, a matchless people!" said Kutuzov; and he closed his eyes and swayed his head. "A matchless people!" he repeated with a sigh.
"So you want to smell gunpowder?" he said to Pierre. "Yes, it's a pleasant smell. I have the honor of being one of your wife's admirers. Is she well? My quarters are at your service."
And as often happens with old people, Kutuzov began looking around absent-mindedly, as if forgetting everything he wanted to say or do.
Then, evidently remembering what he wanted, he beckoned to Andrei Kaisarov, his adjutant's brother.
"Those verses... those verses of Marin's... how do they go? The ones he wrote about Gerakov: 'Lectures for the corps inditing'... Recite them!" said he, clearly preparing to laugh.
Kaisarov recited... Kutuzov nodded his head, smiling, to the rhythm of the verses.
When Pierre had left Kutuzov, Dolokhov came up to him and took his hand.

"I am very glad to meet you here, Count," he said aloud, regardless of strangers present, in a particularly resolute and solemn tone. "On the eve of a day when God alone knows who of us is destined to survive, I'm glad of this chance to tell you that I regret the misunderstandings between us and would wish you not to hold any ill feelings toward me. I beg you to forgive me."
Pierre looked at Dolokhov with a smile, not knowing what to say. With tears in his eyes, Dolokhov embraced Pierre and kissed him.
Boris said a few words to his general, and Count Bennigsen turned to Pierre and proposed that he ride with him along the line.
"It will interest you," he said.
"Yes, very much," replied Pierre.
Half an hour later Kutuzov left for Tatarinova, and Bennigsen and his suite, with Pierre among them, set out on their ride along the line.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter XXIII
paragraphs: From Gorki, Bennigsen descended the highway to the bridge which, when they had looked at it from the hill, the officer had pointed out as the center of our position, and where rows of sweet-smelling new-mown hay lay by the riverside. They rode across that bridge into the village of Borodino and then turned to the left, passing a huge number of troops and guns, and came to a high knoll where militiamen were digging. This was the redoubt, as yet unnamed, which would later be known as the Raevsky Redoubt or the Knoll Battery, but Pierre paid no special attention to it. He didn't know it would become more memorable to him than any other spot on the plain of Borodino.

They then crossed the hollow to Semenovsk, where the soldiers were pulling the last logs from the huts and barns. Then they rode downhill and uphill, across a rye field trampled and beaten down as if by hail, following a track freshly made by the artillery over the furrows of plowed land, and reached some fleches that were still being dug.
* A type of entrenchment.

At the fleches, Bennigsen stopped and began studying the Shevardino Redoubt opposite, which had been ours the day before and where several horsemen could be seen. The officers said that either Napoleon or Murat was there, and they all gazed eagerly at this small group of riders. Pierre also looked at them, trying to guess which of the barely discernible figures was Napoleon. At last those mounted men rode away from the mound and disappeared.

Bennigsen spoke to a general who approached him and began explaining our entire troop positions. Pierre listened, straining every faculty to understand the essential points of the coming battle, but was dismayed to find that his mental capacity was inadequate for the task. He couldn't make sense of it. Bennigsen stopped speaking and, noticing that Pierre was listening, suddenly said to him:
"I don't think this interests you?"
"On the contrary, it's very interesting!" replied Pierre, not quite truthfully.

From the fleches they rode still further to the left, along a road winding through a thick, low-growing birch wood. In the middle of the wood, a brown hare with white feet sprang out and, frightened by the tramping of so many horses, grew so confused that it ran along the road in front of them for some time, attracting general attention and laughter. Only when several voices shouted at it did it dart to one side and disappear in the thicket. After going through the wood for about a mile and a half, they came out on a clearing where troops of Tuchkov's corps were stationed to defend the left flank.

Here, on the extreme left flank, Bennigsen talked at length and with great heat, and, as it seemed to Pierre, gave orders of great military importance. In front of Tuchkov's troops there was a high ground not occupied by troops. Bennigsen loudly criticized this mistake, saying it was madness to leave a height that commanded the surrounding country unoccupied, and to place troops below it. Some of the generals expressed the same opinion. One in particular declared with military passion that they had been placed there to be slaughtered. Bennigsen, on his own authority, ordered the troops to occupy the high ground. This decision on the left flank deepened Pierre's doubts about his own ability to understand military matters. Listening to Bennigsen and the generals criticize the position of the troops behind the hill, he fully understood them and shared their view—but for that very reason couldn't understand how the person who had placed them there behind the hill could have made so obvious a blunder.

Pierre didn't know that these troops were not, as Bennigsen supposed, placed there to defend the position, but were in concealment as an ambush—not meant to be seen—so they could strike an approaching enemy unexpectedly. Bennigsen didn't know this, and moved the troops forward according to his own ideas without consulting the commander in chief.
